title: Comfort ye (Isaiah 40:1–2)
hookLine: after Tisha B'Av, prophetic readings of comfort begin

cards: Chapter thirty-nine of Isaiah holds a warning: the treasures of the king's house will one day be carried off to Babylon. Then chapter forty opens with a different sound entirely.
Two words, the same word twice: Nachamu, nachamu. Comfort, comfort. A Shabbat in the Jewish year is named after that word.
It comes right after Tisha B'Av, the fast of mourning for the fallen Temple, and synagogues read these verses on it. A day of grief, and then, the very next Shabbat, comfort.

teach.b: Here is how the chapter begins, in the King James words: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God." Notice the ye. The command is plural.

God isn't comforting the people directly here; God is telling a group, unnamed, to go and do it. Some readers hear prophets, some hear angels, some hear anyone within earshot. Comfort, in this verse, is a job handed out.
And the word is doubled: once wasn't enough. Then: "Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem." The Hebrew is warmer than the English.
It says, literally, speak to the heart of Jerusalem. Not at her, not about her: to her heart. And what are the comforters told to say?

That her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned, that she has received double for all her sins. This comfort doesn't pretend nothing happened. It names the war and the wrong, and says: it is over now.
That shape lives on in an ordinary Jewish custom.
When people visit a house of mourning, there is a traditional sentence said to the mourners as they leave, asking that God comfort them among the other mourners of Zion and Jerusalem.

teach.h: SPEAK TO THE HEART OF JERUSALEM.
teach.b: Same word for comfort. Same city.

teach.h: IT NAMES THE LOSS, THEN SAYS: IT IS OVER.
teach.b: The private loss in one living room is set beside the old loss of a whole people, and both are spoken to the heart.
Comfort, in this chapter, is less a feeling than a visit.

how: Isaiah 40 is read in synagogue on Shabbat Nachamu, the Shabbat after Tisha B'Av, and Jews visiting a house of mourning traditionally offer a set line of comfort that names the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem.

o: repent: a call to turn back from sin
mourning: the fast for the fallen Temple
comfort, comfort: a doubled call to console

s: in Isaiah 40, God comforts the people directly
God tells a group to do it: comfort ye. the comfort is a job handed out.
the comfort pretends nothing was lost
it names the war and the wrong, then says it is over.
a Shabbat is named after this verse's first word
Shabbat Nachamu, right after Tisha B'Av.

games.q: you're the prophet. the warnings came true, and the people are grieving. what is your first word to them?
o: a long explanation of why it happened.
games.why: "comfort ye, comfort ye my people." the chapter after a warning opens with the same word twice.

practice: Let someone come to mind who is carrying something heavy right now, a loss, a diagnosis, a long hard season, and don't try to solve it.
Ask what speaking to their heart would sound like: not advice, not a reason, maybe just I'm thinking of you, I'm here. If you pray, you can hold the verse's two words for them: comfort, comfort.

wordCard.voice: Nachamu. Comfort ye, a plural command, said twice at the start of Isaiah forty, and the name of the Shabbat after Tisha B'Av. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: comfort, comfort my people, the opening of Isaiah 40.

carryVoice: Your line: comfort ye my people. The command is plural, and it's said twice. Seven hundred eighty-seven days now.
